history.heading: The Ellice Islands
paragraphs: Tuvalu, nine small coral islands and atolls in the central Pacific, was settled by Polynesians, mainly from Samoa and Tonga, over 2,000 years ago. In the 1860s Peruvian slave raiders kidnapped hundreds of people, and disease further reduced the population. Missionaries converted most islanders to Christianity.

Britain declared a protectorate over the islands, then called the Ellice Islands, in 1892, governing them with the Gilbert Islands (now Kiribati). After a 1974 referendum, the Ellice Islands separated and became independent as Tuvalu on 1 October 1978.

culture.heading: Island traditions
paragraphs: Tuvaluan and English are spoken. Most people belong to the Church of Tuvalu. Fatele, a dance with singing and drumming, and the community meeting house (maneapa) are central to life. Pulaka (swamp taro), coconut and fish are staples. With about 11,000 people, Tuvalu is one of the world's least populous countries.

politics.heading: Parliamentary democracy
paragraphs: Tuvalu is a parliamentary democracy and Commonwealth realm with the British monarch as head of state. There are no political parties; the 16 members of parliament elect the prime minister. Tuvalu recognises Taiwan.
In 2023 Tuvalu signed the Falepili Union treaty with Australia, which offers Tuvaluans a pathway to migrate to Australia because of climate change and gives Australia a role in Tuvalu's security.

economy.heading: Ocean and climate
paragraphs: Tuvalu's economy depends on fishing licences, the Tuvalu Trust Fund, foreign aid, remittances and revenue from its internet domain, .tv. With a highest point just a few metres above sea level, Tuvalu is among the countries most threatened by rising seas, and it is creating a digital copy of itself to preserve its culture. The currency is the Australian dollar.
